passage.title: The Blue Flame of Murano
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Sparks danced above the brick furnace as Nico turned the long iron blowpipe in his blistered hands. On the island of Murano in 1510, glassmakers lived under strict laws. Their roaring ovens had been moved across the bay from Venice to stop city fires. That move also helped guard the guild's coveted recipes. Nico worked as a young helper to Master Lorenzo. The old man was the only one who knew how to melt sand, ash, and ground blue stone into luminous cobalt glass. Kings across Europe paid gold coins for a single blue goblet from Lorenzo's shop.

Each night after the coals cooled, Nico swept the stone floor and watched over the small back room. Late one foggy evening, the locked cedar chest holding the master's mineral ledger was quietly pried open by a rival merchant from the mainland. Nico heard the sharp click of the iron latch from the hall. Peering through a crack in the door, he saw a cloaked man copy a page by candle flame. Then the thief slipped out toward the canal dock. Nico's heart raced, yet when he checked the open chest, he let out a slow breath of relief.

Two weeks earlier, Master Lorenzo had warned Nico that spies were bribing boatmen along the dock. Together, they had prepared a clever decoy book and placed it inside the carved cedar chest. That false page listed common river sand and gray lead ore. In a hot kiln, that mix would only bake into dull, cloudy mud. Meanwhile, the genuine formula for cobalt blue was not written on paper at all. Instead, Lorenzo had taught Nico to read the recipe from a row of colored glass beads strung on a copper wire above the workbench.

Each bead on that wire stood for a set weight of blue ore, white quartz, and sea-plant ash. To a stranger, the wire looked like a string of scrap beads left over from old necklaces. To Nico, the order of small and large beads told the exact count of scoops needed for the batch. Even if a thief stole the wire, the beads meant nothing without knowing which clay scoop matched each color.

When Master Lorenzo arrived at dawn, Nico showed him the scratched lock on the chest. Then he pointed to the safe wire above the bench. The old man clapped Nico on the shoulder and handed him the main blowpipe for the morning melt. Nico dipped the hot iron tip into the glowing pot and gathered a globe of deep blue glass. As he blew air through the pipe, the cup swelled like a dark ocean wave catching the sun.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Late one foggy evening, the locked cedar chest holding the master's mineral ledger was quietly pried open by a rival merchant from the mainland."

Based on the structure of this sentence, who or what actually opened the cedar chest?

options.text: A rival merchant from the mainland
The master's mineral ledger inside the box
The thick evening fog rolling in from the canal
A boatman who worked at the Venice dock

questions.provingSentenceText: Late one foggy evening, the locked cedar chest holding the master's mineral ledger was quietly pried open by a rival merchant from the mainland.
questions.childTip: Find the 'by' phrase after 'was quietly pried open' to see who did the prying.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'the locked cedar chest' is the receiver of the action and 'holding the master's mineral ledger' is a modifier. The true actor comes after 'by': 'a rival merchant from the mainland' (Option B).

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Together, they had prepared a clever decoy book and placed it inside the carved cedar chest."

What does the word "decoy" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: An ancient ledger written in gold ink by a king
A fake item left out to trick a thief and protect the real secret
A heavy iron lock that cannot be broken with tools
A complete collection of every glass recipe on Murano Island

questions.provingSentenceText: Together, they had prepared a clever decoy book and placed it inside the carved cedar chest.
questions.childTip: Read the next sentence in Paragraph 3 about the 'false page' to see what kind of book they put in the chest.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains that the book in the chest contained a 'false page' with common river sand while the 'genuine formula' was hidden elsewhere, proving that 'decoy' means a fake item used to trick someone (Option C).

questions.prompt: Why does Nico feel relief instead of panic when he checks the open chest at the end of Paragraph 2?

options.text: He realizes that the candle flame burned up the thief's copy before the man reached the dock.
He sees that the cloaked man accidentally dropped a bag of gold coins into the chest.
He knows the thief only copied a fake recipe while the real formula remained hidden in the glass beads.
He wants the mainland merchant to teach everyone in Venice how to make cobalt glass.

questions.provingSentenceText: Meanwhile, the genuine formula for cobalt blue was not written on paper at all.
questions.childTip: Click the sentence in Paragraph 3 that explains why the real cobalt blue formula was safe from paper thieves.
questions.parentExplanation: Nico feels relief because he and Master Lorenzo had placed a decoy ledger in the chest two weeks earlier, while the genuine formula was never written on paper at all (Option A).

questions.prompt: How do Paragraphs 2 and 3 work together to build suspense and then resolve it?

options.text: Paragraph 2 introduces Master Lorenzo's childhood, while Paragraph 3 skips ahead fifty years.
Paragraph 2 describes how to blow a glass goblet, while Paragraph 3 lists the kings who bought them.
Paragraph 2 explains why Venice banned fires, while Paragraph 3 shows the furnace burning down the shop.
Paragraph 2 shows a break-in that makes it seem the secret was stolen, while Paragraph 3 flashes back to explain the trap set two weeks earlier.

questions.provingSentenceText: Two weeks earlier, Master Lorenzo had warned Nico that spies were bribing boatmen along the dock.
questions.childTip: Notice how Paragraph 2 ends with a surprising sigh of relief, and Paragraph 3 steps back 'Two weeks earlier' to explain why.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RL5, Paragraph 2 creates dramatic tension when a spy copies the ledger from the chest, and Paragraph 3 shifts back two weeks earlier to reveal how Lorenzo and Nico had planted a decoy book (Option A).

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses a central theme of the story?

options.text: Clever preparation and shared trust can protect valuable knowledge better than a heavy lock alone.
Apprentices should never be allowed to learn how a master craftsperson mixes materials.
Every secret formula should be carved into stone walls so nobody can carry it away.
Common river sand and gray lead ore make the brightest blue glass in Europe.

questions.provingSentenceText: Instead, Lorenzo had taught Nico to read the recipe from a row of colored glass beads strung on a copper wire above the workbench.
questions.childTip: Think about how Lorenzo and Nico outsmarted the spy when the iron latch on the chest failed.
questions.parentExplanation: Although the spy easily pried open the iron lock on the cedar chest, Lorenzo and Nico protected the formula through foresight—hiding the recipe in plain sight on a bead wire that only they understood (Option A).

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Sparks danced above the brick furnace as Nico turned the long iron blowpipe in his blistered hands."
"Kings across Europe paid gold coins for a single blue goblet from Lorenzo's shop."
"Instead, Lorenzo had taught Nico to read the recipe from a row of colored glass beads strung on a copper wire above the workbench."
"Nico dipped the hot iron tip into the glowing pot and gathered a globe of deep blue glass."

questions.provingSentenceText: Instead, Lorenzo had taught Nico to read the recipe from a row of colored glass beads strung on a copper wire above the workbench.
questions.childTip: Pick the quote that shows how the master and apprentice hid the real recipe using shared knowledge.
questions.parentExplanation: Option C directly proves the theme in Part A by showing how Master Lorenzo trusted Nico with the coded bead system that kept the recipe safe even after the chest was pried open.
